documentNotes.title: Read once more before you start your work
documentNotes.statement:
**General note.** Maybe not all problems have correct questions. Some questions (maybe the main question of the problem, maybe one of the subquestions) may make no real sense. In this case you have to write in your answer (in English or Russian): «impossible situation – ситуация невозможна». Of course, this answer has to be explained numerically or logically.

**Data from the tables** (Planetary data, stars, constants, etc.) may be used for solving every problem.

The answers «Да-Yes» or «Нет-No» have to be written in English or Russian.

**Ещё раз прочитайте перед началом работы.**

**Общее замечание.** Не исключено, что не во всех задачах вопросы поставлены корректно. Некоторые вопросы (возможно, главный вопрос задачи, возможно – подвопрос) могут не иметь смысла. В этом случае следует написать в ответе (по-русски или по-английски): «ситуация невозможна – impossible situation». Естественно, ответ должен быть подкреплён вычислениями или логическими рассуждениями.

**Данные из таблиц** (Солнечная система, звёзды, константы) могут быть использованы в любой задаче.

Ответы «Да-Yes» или «Нет-No» должны быть написаны по-русски или по-английски.

problems.statement:
Yesterday, on October 16, 2015, the upper culmination of the Sun at the venue of the Olympiad was at 11:29:43 local time. Calculate as accurate as possible at what time the upper culmination of the Sun will be (or was) today.

Estimate the difference $\Delta h$ in the height of the Sun at the culminations yesterday and today.

solution.statement:
**Official sketches for solutions; for jury work only.** The given sketches are not full; team leaders have to give more detailed explanations to students. Correct solutions in students' papers (enough for 8 points) may be shorter.

**Jury note.** Evaluate the solution in essence, not by formal existence of mentioned sentences or formulae. Their formal presence is not necessary to give the respective points. Give points if the following steps de facto use these positions.

The first source page prints these notes twice, under both “Sketches for solutions” and “Basic criteria”. No item-by-item numerical grading breakdown appears in the archived five images. The running headers on images 2–4 print “XX IAO 2014”, while their footers and the cover identify 2015.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
From the graph of the Equation of Time we see that now (and until approximately the first days of November) the apparent noon (the culmination of the Sun) every day comes a little earlier. We can find the rate by drawing a tangent to the curve at today's date. The rate is −30 minutes in about 5 months, or about −12 seconds per day.

So the upper culmination today will be at 11:29:43 − 00:00:12 = **11:29:31**.

The difference in height is equal to the change of the declination of the Sun during the day. The source writes $\Delta h=\Delta\varepsilon$ at this point, then denotes declination by $\delta$ below. An easy approximation for the current season is

$$\delta=-\varepsilon\sin B,$$

where $\varepsilon=23^\circ26'$; $B$ is an analog of angle, $2\pi\sim360^\circ\sim365.25$ days, starting at the autumn equinox (this year about noon on September 23). With $N$ the number of days since September 23,

$$\delta=-\varepsilon\sin\frac{2\pi N}{365.25},\qquad \frac{d\delta}{dN}=-\frac{2\pi}{365.25}\varepsilon\cos\frac{2\pi N}{365.25}.$$

For today $N=24$, giving $d\delta/dN=-0.37^\circ\approx-22'$. So the Sun today culminates **22′ lower** than yesterday.

problems.statement:
The White Bear and the Penguin from the previous International Astronomy Olympiads returned to their poles (North and South respectively), and decided to observe an annular solar eclipse. The Penguin was lucky to see an amazing picture: at the maximum phase of the eclipse the centres of both discs, solar and lunar, appeared just on the visible horizon. And what did the Bear observe at this time? Draw what the White Bear saw at that moment, and also contour by dotted line the true positions of the Sun and the Moon.

Assume that the Earth is spherical. The drawing should include an artistic picture with an image of the Bear on North Pole; necessary sizes or angular sizes should be pointed out in the picture. Recollect for yourself the necessary information about the animals.

solution.statement:
**Official sketches for solutions; for jury work only.** The given sketches are not full; team leaders have to give more detailed explanations to students. Correct solutions in students' papers (enough for 8 points) may be shorter.

**Jury note.** Evaluate the solution in essence, not by formal existence of mentioned sentences or formulae. Their formal presence is not necessary to give the respective points. Give points if the following steps de facto use these positions.

The first source page prints these notes twice, under both “Sketches for solutions” and “Basic criteria”. No item-by-item numerical grading breakdown appears in the archived five images. The running headers on images 2–4 print “XX IAO 2014”, while their footers and the cover identify 2015.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
It seems that since the points of observations are opposite, the situation should be absolutely symmetric: the White Bear should also observe half of the eclipsed solar disk on the horizon. But this is quite incorrect. Three circumstances must be taken into account.

**Horizon depression.** For any observer the physical horizon is slightly lowered. A person standing on a flat surface sees about 2.5′ depression. For Earth's radius $R$ and eye height $h$, the horizon dip is

$$\arccos\frac{R}{R+h}\approx\frac{\sqrt{(R+h)^2-R^2}}R\approx\sqrt{\frac{2h}R}\quad\text{(radians)}.$$

Take an Imperial Penguin with eyes about 1 m above the surface: depression about 2′. The White Bear is sitting, with eyes also about 1 m high, so depression about 2′ (standing, more than 2 m and about 3′). If the Penguin sees the solar centre on its horizon, it is already 2′ below the mathematical horizon. At the North Pole it is 2′ above the mathematical horizon, or 4′ above the sitting Bear's physical horizon — a quarter of the solar radius. Horizon depression is the smallest effect here.

**Atmospheric refraction.** This varies slightly with the weather, averaging about 35′ at the horizon. When the solar centre is visible on the South Pole horizon, at the North Pole it can be seen well above the horizon. Refraction at the South Pole contributes 35′, and at the North Pole about 25′ (not 35′, since the Sun is higher). This is still not the principal effect.

**Lunar parallax.** An annular eclipse is visible only in a narrow band on Earth. The distance to the Moon is 384 thousand km. The source then calls 12730 km the Earth's “polar radius” and prints

$$12730/38400\approx0.0332\ \mathrm{rad}\approx1.9^\circ.$$

*Source discrepancy: the printed 12730 km is a diameter, and the denominator 38400 lacks a zero relative to the preceding lunar distance. The printed numerical angular result is retained.*

The Bear does **not observe any solar eclipse**, neither annular nor partial. The solar centre is about $4'+35'+25'=64'$ (about 1°) above the horizon. The lunar disk is approximately 1°54′ below the solar one, totally below the horizon. More precisely this is 1°54′ below the true solar position; including refraction, the true Moon is 2°19′ below the apparent Sun.

problems.statement: Some time after the events described in the previous problem (nobody knows even the order of magnitude how long after – minutes, or hours, or days, or years ...), Venus at the point of eastern elongation came to close conjunction with Mars, which was located near the aphelion of its orbit. At the same time a total lunar eclipse occurred on the Earth.

parts.statement: Explain, which animal (sitting at the same poles) may see this lunar eclipse. (At the very end of your explanation write as answer **B+** or **B−** for the Bear and **P+** or **P−** for the Penguin.) An artistic picture of the observations of the animals is welcome.
Calculate in which constellation the eclipsed Moon was observed.
Estimate minimal possible time passed from the situation of the previous problem to the situation of the current one.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
**3.1.** The corresponding scheme is supplied separately in the archive.

![Official conjunction diagram: Sun, Earth, Moon, Venus, Mars, angles α β γ and directions1 and2](#p3-conjunction-astra-s9-r1)

The angles are

$$\alpha=\arccos\frac{A_V}{(1+e)A_M}=\arccos\frac{0.723}{1.093\cdot1.524}=64.3^\circ,$$

$$\beta=\arccos\frac{A_V}{A_E}=\arccos\frac{0.723}{1}=43.7^\circ.$$

The source prints the following chain for the third angle:

$$\gamma=180^\circ-\alpha-\beta=\arccos(A_V/A_E)=\arccos(0.723/1)=72^\circ.$$

*Source discrepancy: the two arccos expressions repeat the preceding β calculation, while 72° belongs to $180^\circ-\alpha-\beta$.*

**3.3.** Mars is at aphelion, opposite its perihelion position. Mars at perihelion may be in great opposition for Earth observers in late August (August 25). Direction 1 (Mars→Sun) therefore corresponds to Sun→Earth on August 25. Direction 2 corresponds to Sun→Earth 72° earlier, or 71 days earlier, June 15. By the sky map this direction is in **Ophiuchus**, near the Sagittarius border.

**3.2.** The situation is thus in mid-June. The Sun shines for the Bear at the North Pole, while the Moon, on the opposite side of the celestial sphere during eclipse, can be observed by the Penguin at the South Pole. Answer: **B− P+**.

**3.4.** The first situation was near equinox, the second in mid-June. Both require the Moon near its orbital nodes. The nodes move in the opposite direction with a period of 18.6 years. The minimum interval can occur if the line of nodes moves from the end-September/end-March line to the mid-June/mid-December line, about 28% of a period:

$$18.6\cdot0.28=5.2\ \text{years}.$$

Thus the minimum is about 5 years and almost 2–3 months. In 5 years and exactly 3 months the number of synodic lunar periods is

$$(365.25\cdot5.25)/29.53=64.94.$$

For our situations it should be an integer and a half:

$$64.5\cdot29.53=1904.7\ \text{days}.$$

The source checks against March 20, 2015 (total solar eclipse near the North Pole and equinox). 1904.7 days later is June 5–6, 2020. It says that a lunar eclipse, “although not full but partial”, will occur on June 5 evening, with the Moon in Sagittarius. *This is the source's approximate check, explicitly not the total lunar eclipse assumed in the question; no stronger agreement is claimed.*

problems.statement: According to an ancient legend of Middle Volga there was a constellation called White Leopard (Белый Барс – Pardus Album) in the sky in the very past, in which the number of stars were exactly equal to the number of letters in the Greek alphabet, and the stars had magnitudes $\alpha$ PaA – $+0.10^{m}$, $\beta$ PaA – $+0.20^{m}$, $\gamma$ PaA – $+0.30^{m}$, $\delta$ PaA – $+0.40^{m}$, and so on with adding $0.10^{m}$ till $\omega$ PaA. Calculate the total magnitude of the stars of this constellation.

solution.statement:
**Official sketches for solutions; for jury work only.** The given sketches are not full; team leaders have to give more detailed explanations to students. Correct solutions in students' papers (enough for 8 points) may be shorter.

**Jury note.** Evaluate the solution in essence, not by formal existence of mentioned sentences or formulae. Their formal presence is not necessary to give the respective points. Give points if the following steps de facto use these positions.

The first source page prints these notes twice, under both “Sketches for solutions” and “Basic criteria”. No item-by-item numerical grading breakdown appears in the archived five images. The running headers on images 2–4 print “XX IAO 2014”, while their footers and the cover identify 2015.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
There are 24 letters in the Greek alphabet, so take the 24 magnitudes from +0.10 to +2.40.

The source first jokes: $0.10+0.20+\cdots+2.40=12\cdot2.50=30$ magnitudes — “Sorry, a joke.”

Really we must add to the first star's flux the other 23 fluxes, decreasing exponentially with pitch

$$10^{0.4\cdot0.10}\approx1.09648.$$

The infinite sum can be found by a geometric progression. The source prints

$$\Phi(1\text{–}\infty)=\Phi(1)+\Phi(\infty)/1.09648,$$

$$\Phi(1\text{–}\infty)=\Phi(\infty)/1.04713=\Phi(1),$$

$$\Phi(1\text{–}\infty)=\frac{\Phi(1)}{1-1/1.04713}=\Phi(1)\cdot11.37.$$

*Source discrepancies: the middle line is printed as an equality chain, and the subsequent denominator uses 1.04713 instead of the preceding pitch 1.09648. The printed multiplier 11.37 follows the latter pitch.*

The magnitude of the infinite series would be

$$m(1\text{–}\infty)=0.10-2.5\log11.37\approx-2.54.$$

There are only 24 stars. Subtract the flux of the analogous infinite series starting at the 25th star, magnitude 2.50. Every star in this second series is 2.40 magnitudes weaker; so is the series as a whole:

$$m(25\text{–}\infty)=2.50-2.5\log11.37\approx-0.14.$$

The source jokes again about subtracting magnitudes: $-2.54-(-0.14)=-2.40$ — “Sorry, a joke once again.” Fluxes must instead be subtracted. The second flux is $10^{0.4\cdot2.4}\approx9.12$ times weaker:

$$\Phi(25\text{–}\infty)=\frac{\Phi(1\text{–}\infty)}{10^{0.96}}=\frac{\Phi(1)\cdot11.37}{9.12}\approx\Phi(1)\cdot1.246,$$

$$\Phi(1\text{–}24)=\Phi(1\text{–}\infty)-\Phi(25\text{–}\infty)=\Phi(1)(11.37-1.246)=\Phi(1)\cdot10.12.$$

Hence

$$\boxed{m(1\text{–}24)=0.10-2.5\log10.12\approx-2.41.}$$

**Attention!** The second joke happens to give almost the right number, by pure coincidence. Not any solution giving the same numerical value is right; pay attention when checking.

**Other approaches.** Calculate each star's flux, add the fluxes, and recover the total apparent magnitude. A proper calculation gives exactly the same answer (easy to check in Excel), but is lengthy without a computer or programmable calculator.

A very rough linear approximation uses the “average” magnitude $(0.10+2.40)/2=1.25$, giving

$$1.25-2.5\log24\approx1.25-3.45=-2.20.$$

The source says this is very rough and not suitable as a workable solution, but “a little better than nothing”.

problems.title: Constellation of White Leopard

problems.statement: A spiral galaxy consisting mainly of A7-A8 spectral class stars was discovered in the Southern Cross (Crux) constellation. The galaxy may be seen as oval of about 40 by 30 arcsec in the sky. The broadened H$\alpha$ line is observed at wavelengths approximately from 7054 Å to 7057 Å in the spectrum of the galaxy. Other lines in the spectrum are also shifted and broadened proportionally. Estimate the number of stars in the galaxy.

solution.statement:
**Official sketches for solutions; for jury work only.** The given sketches are not full; team leaders have to give more detailed explanations to students. Correct solutions in students' papers (enough for 8 points) may be shorter.

**Jury note.** Evaluate the solution in essence, not by formal existence of mentioned sentences or formulae. Their formal presence is not necessary to give the respective points. Give points if the following steps de facto use these positions.

The first source page prints these notes twice, under both “Sketches for solutions” and “Basic criteria”. No item-by-item numerical grading breakdown appears in the archived five images. The running headers on images 2–4 print “XX IAO 2014”, while their footers and the cover identify 2015.

sections.title: Solution
sections.statement:
First, the values are given with accuracy of one digit, and the wavelength difference can also be obtained with only one digit, so a more accurate final answer is inappropriate. The redshift is $z=\Delta\lambda/\lambda\approx0.075$, so the galaxy recedes with $v=zc=22500$ km/s. By Hubble's law, with $H=68$ km/s/Mpc,

$$L=v/H=zc/H\approx320\ \mathrm{Mpc}.$$

The angular size is 40″, so the source prints

$$D=(40/205265)\cdot320\ \mathrm{Mpc}\approx62\ \mathrm{kpc}=1.9\cdot10^{21}\ \mathrm m,$$

$$R=D/2=31\ \mathrm{kpc}=1.0\cdot10^{21}\ \mathrm m.$$

*The denominator 205265 is printed in the source.*

The spiral galaxy appears elliptical, so its plane is inclined to the line of sight at angle $\alpha$:

$$\cos\alpha=30/40,\qquad\alpha\approx41^\circ.$$

The spectral broadening is due to stellar motion. The solution text gives a range 6854 Å to 6857 Å, a broadening of 1.5 Å in either direction. The radial speed of the outermost stars is

$$V_R=(1.5\ \mathring{\mathrm A}/7055\ \mathring{\mathrm A})c=64\ \mathrm{km/s},$$

and their total speed is

$$V=V_R/\sin\alpha=96\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$

*Source discrepancy: the solution prose says 6854–6857 Å, while the question says 7054–7057 Å and the solution's velocity calculation uses 7055 Å.*

Assume the outermost stars move in circular orbits with this speed and the galactic mass is concentrated at the centre. Kepler's law gives

$$V^2/R=GM/R^2,\qquad M=V^2R/G=1.34\cdot10^{41}\ \mathrm{kg}.$$

For stars of spectral class A7–A8 take Altair as typical, with mass 1.7 solar masses, or $3.4\cdot10^{30}$ kg. Then

$$N=M/M_A\approx4\cdot10^{10},$$

or **about 40 billion stars**.
